title: Air India Seeks $1.5 Billion in Fresh Equity From Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines as Losses Mount
excerpt: The carrier's combined FY26 losses topped $2.3 billion, drawing political scrutiny in Singapore and raising questions about the decade-long turnaround timeline.
body:
• Air India is seeking approximately $1.5 billion in fresh equity from Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, one of its largest reported shareholder funding requests since the Tata Group took control in 2022.
  • The carrier and its budget arm Air India Express posted combined losses of $2.33 billion in the fiscal year ended March 2026, more than double the prior year.
  • Singapore Airlines, which holds a 25% stake, faces political pressure at home after a Singapore opposition lawmaker questioned the use of Temasek funds to shore up the loss-making Indian carrier.
  • Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran, who is set to step down in February, has said the turnaround could take up to a decade.

Air India is seeking about $1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, months after the second-largest Indian airline posted a record annual loss, according to a Reuters report citing two people familiar with the matter.

The proposed capital infusion would rank among Air India's largest publicly reported requests for shareholder funding since the Tata Group took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022. It underscores the scale of the financial challenge involved in rebuilding the airline while simultaneously investing in its fleet, operations, technology, and customer proposition.

"Air India wants the funds immediately, though the infusion is likely to happen in tranches. Singapore Airlines would need to contribute its share of the proposed infusion for the investment to go through."

— Source familiar with the matter, speaking to Reuters

Record Losses Pile Pressure on Turnaround

Air India and its budget subsidiary Air India Express posted combined losses of $2.33 billion for the fiscal year ended March 2026, more than double the losses recorded the previous year. The scale of the red ink has weighed on Singapore Airlines' own profits — the Singapore carrier reported a $945.2 million loss from its Air India investment in FY26, according to Entrepreneur India.

https://x.com/IndiaInfraTech/status/2093632113929240596

The airline's financial woes have been compounded by a string of external disruptions. Pakistan's airspace ban on Indian carriers has forced costly rerouting of flights. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted Air India's international network. And the fallout from a deadly crash last year that killed 260 people continues to shadow the airline's recovery efforts.

A Decade-Long Transformation

Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran, who is preparing to step down in February following reported disagreements with the group's controlling charitable trust — partly over Air India's losses — has said the airline's turnaround could take up to a decade. The transformation involves overhauling legacy IT systems, organizational culture, and a fleet that is being both refurbished and expanded.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=tK9MlFk1nEY

Air India has also sought to defer deliveries of hundreds of jets ordered from Airbus and Boeing as Tata presses the carrier to cut costs. Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong has described the turnaround as a "long game," stressing there is no shortcut to rebuilding the airline.

"Air India is expected to continue requiring capital infusions in the coming years."

— Source familiar with the matter, speaking to Reuters

Political Pushback in Singapore

The funding request has drawn political scrutiny beyond India's borders. Kenneth Tiong, a Workers' Party member of Singapore's parliament, publicly opposed the use of state investor Temasek's funds to shore up Air India. Since Temasek majority-owns Singapore Airlines, which in turn holds a 25.1% stake in Air India, any equity contribution flows indirectly from Singapore's sovereign wealth.

"I will not support, nor expect, any future use of Temasek's funds to prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines," Tiong said in a social media post, according to Reuters. He has filed a question for oral answer in parliament on September 8, asking whether the transport minister has assessed the impact of losses from Singapore Airlines' foreign associates on its capacity to provide essential transport services.

What Comes Next

Discussions between Air India, Tata Sons, and Singapore Airlines remain ongoing, with no final decision taken on the amount or timing of the equity infusion. The capital is being sought in the form of fresh equity rather than debt, and is expected to arrive in tranches rather than a single injection.

Air India's trajectory will depend not only on securing the funding but on broader factors: whether the airline's fleet modernization begins generating returns, whether geopolitical disruptions ease, and whether the incoming Tata Sons leadership maintains the current transformation strategy. For now, the message from inside the airline is clear — the turnaround remains expensive, and the tab is growing.
